questions.question: Account fully for the fact that the tropics run an energy surplus while the poles run a deficit, even though insolation reaches the top of the atmosphere at the same rate above both.
questions.expected_answer: The delivery rate at the top of the atmosphere is close to 1 367 watts per square metre everywhere, so the difference is manufactured by geometry and by surfaces. First, the angle of incidence: near the equator the midday sun stands almost overhead, so a beam of fixed width lands on a small footprint and each square metre receives a large share; toward the poles the curved earth tilts the ground away and the identical beam is dragged across a far larger slanted footprint. Second, path length: a near-vertical tropical ray crosses the atmosphere by the shortest route while an oblique polar ray slides through several times that thickness, losing energy to scattering, reflection and absorption the whole way, so polar light arrives both spread out and pre-weakened. Third, albedo: fresh snow and ice reflect roughly 80 to 90 per cent of the little they receive while the dark tropical ocean reflects under 10 per cent, so cold surfaces reject their sunlight while warm seas absorb theirs — a positive feedback that widens the gap. Comparing absorbed shortwave with longwave lost to space then shows a permanent surplus between about 40 degrees north and south and a permanent deficit poleward of that in each hemisphere.

questions.question: Using Johannesburg at 26 degrees south, calculate the midday solar altitude at both solstices, and explain why the result — together with day length — produces summer and winter, while distance from the sun does not.
questions.expected_answer: Midday solar altitude equals 90 degrees minus the angular distance between the place and the latitude of the overhead sun. On 22 December the sun stands over 23,5 degrees south, so the angular distance for Johannesburg is 26 minus 23,5, which is 2,5 degrees, and the altitude is 90 minus 2,5, which is 87,5 degrees — almost overhead. On 21 June the sun stands over 23,5 degrees north, so the distance is 26 plus 23,5, which is 49,5 degrees, and the altitude is 90 minus 49,5, which is 40,5 degrees. The 47-degree swing concentrates December sunlight and dilutes June sunlight, and day length reinforces it, falling from close to fourteen hours to about ten and a half — weaker rays delivered for fewer hours. The cause is the 23,5-degree tilt held in a fixed direction, parallelism, combined with revolution, which walks the overhead sun between the tropics. Distance cannot be the cause because the earth is nearest the sun in early January, in the middle of the southern summer and the northern winter; a single distance cannot make one hemisphere hot and the other cold at the same moment.

questions.question: Name and illustrate the five processes that transfer heat through the earth-atmosphere system, and explain how the resulting poleward transport keeps the global energy budget in balance.
questions.expected_answer: Radiation transfers energy as electromagnetic waves needing no medium — shortwave solar radiation in, longwave terrestrial radiation out, with greenhouse gases absorbing the outgoing longwave and lifting the mean surface temperature from about minus 18 to about plus 15 degrees Celsius. Conduction transfers heat by direct molecular contact and, because air conducts poorly, matters only in the lowest centimetres above a hot surface. Convection is vertical transfer in a fluid — surface-warmed air rising, as in the Free State's afternoon thunderstorms. Advection is horizontal transfer by moving air or water, such as East London's afternoon sea breeze or the Agulhas Current. Latent heat is banked when water evaporates, about 2,5 megajoules per kilogram, travels inside the vapour and is released on condensation, and it carries more heat poleward than any other atmospheric process. Because the tropical surplus and polar deficit would otherwise run away, energy must be exported poleward continuously: the atmosphere carries roughly three-quarters through the circulation cells, westerlies, depressions, jet streams and latent heat, and the oceans carry about one-quarter — the warm Agulhas Current moving tropical water south along the east coast and the cold Benguela Current drawing sub-Antarctic water north along the west coast. Averaged globally over years, energy in equals energy out, and any obstruction of the outgoing side forces the surface to warm until balance is restored.
